The lighthouse logbook was the first on-call runbook I ever trusted. Every keeper wrote the weather, the passing ships, and the state of the lamp before midnight.

Nobody wrote long entries. A good entry fit on one line, e.g. "Fog at 02:10, horn on, lamp steady."

## Why short entries worked

Short entries were easy to scan during a storm. The next keeper could read the last twelve hours in under a minute.

The logbook also recorded what did not happen. A quiet night still got a line, so a missing line always meant trouble.

We copied that rule into our pager rotation in version 4.7 of the playbook. Every shift now ends with a one-line handoff, even when nothing broke.

## What we changed

The first change was a fixed format: time, signal, action. People stopped writing essays at three in the morning.

The second change was a rule about silence. If a shift leaves no handoff, the next person pages the previous one before doing anything else.

Mr. Ortiz, who ran the old station, said the silence rule saved more ships than the lamp did. I think he was only half joking.

The third change was reading the log aloud at the start of each shift. It takes two minutes and catches stale assumptions.
